source.title: Aligning Large Language Models and Geometric Deep Models for Protein Representation
source.authors: Dong Shu; Bingbing Duan; Kai Guo; Kaixiong Zhou; Jiliang Tang; Mengnan Du

record.tranche_reason: The study measures cross-modal alignment and shows that it varies by model pair and protein rarity, including model pairs with scores near zero or below zero. This qualifies broad claims of convergence, although it studies protein text and structure rather than the cited vision-language setting.
record.gate_note: The study's own alignment scores and its stated popular-versus-rare comparison are included. It also reports dimension, projection-head, fine-tuning, reweighting, and downstream-task results; those are not all extracted as rows because the 60-row limit prioritizes the model-pair scores and the reported rarity dependence. Cited background findings are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: New setting: protein text (LLM final-token embeddings) versus protein structure (GDM embeddings). Linear heads are trained contrastively and alignment is scored on held-out proteins. This gives results on scale (V1), linear mappability (V4), input dependence (V6) and incompleteness (V7). The alignment is learned rather than intrinsic, the study does not engage the Platonic hypothesis, and it does not argue against convergence, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that geometry-aware GDMs (GearNet, ScanNet) and larger LLMs align better, and that rarity matters most among protein properties, which they attribute to database imbalance and homology. Higher GDM dimension, 2-layer heads and protein fine-tuning improve alignment. They add that higher alignment yields better downstream description and fewer hallucinations.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses learned projection heads and a contrastive cosine-similarity objective to align protein text and structural representations, rather than directly reproducing either named original source's method.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment varies with the LLM-GDM pair and protein rarity. The paper also reports that GDM embedding dimension, projection-head depth, LLM fine-tuning, and rare-protein reweighting change alignment, but detailed results for those analyses are not extracted as rows here.

fits_no_version.finding: Downstream protein-description ROUGE/BLEU tracks alignment score: GearNet/ScanNet pairs and larger LLMs score higher (Table 2), and retrieval and reweighting improve scores (Tables 3-4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Better cross-modal representation alignment predicts better downstream generation and less hallucination.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-protein alignment scores correlate highly across trained pairs sharing a GDM and across high-alignment pairs (Fig 2B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Proteins that align well in one model pair align well in others.

record.problems: The study uses one alignment metric and reports no uncertainty estimates for the Table 1 scores. The popularity/rarity analysis uses 10 proteins in each group, and its per-protein results are presented in a figure without numeric values in the text. The tested scale comparison varies LLM size in this protein setting and does not establish a general scale law across architectures, objectives, data, and modalities.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit was not reached, but the paper's additional results are not extracted here: GearNet dimension sweep (Figure 2C); projection-head-depth comparisons (Figure 4A and Figure S6B); LLM fine-tuning comparisons (Figure 4B); reweighting scores (Table 3); and downstream ROUGE/BLEU and retrieval results (Tables 2 and 4). These concern alignment strategies or downstream task performance rather than additional model-pair scale or rarity conditions represented above.

untested.parts: Only the LLM side is scaled; pretrained GDMs are fixed. Size is confounded with model family and projection output dimension. No capability measure and no intrinsic (training-free) similarity metric such as mutual kNN or CKA.
No stitching, relative representations or unpaired mapping.
No comparison of similarity metrics or neighbour settings; no out-of-distribution test.
No plateau test; no causal isolation of shared data or objectives.

missing.what: GearNet retrained at dimensions 64 to 3072: alignment rises with GDM embedding dimension for all LLMs, and LLaMa-8B beats Gemma only above 512 dims.
Positive scores rise and negative scores fall with LLM size for GearNet/ScanNet; for GAT, negative scores exceed positive.
2-layer projection heads significantly beat 1-layer (linear) heads for all pairs; a third layer gives marginal or negative change.
Fine-tuning LLMs on protein descriptions raises alignment for all pairs.
Reweighting rare proteins raises alignment scores, e.g. ScanNet-70B +0.0496.

record.verdict_notes: Alignment here is induced by contrastively trained projection heads; only the held-out generalization of that map is measured, so it bears mainly on V4. It is not a training-free similarity measure of the Platonic-hypothesis kind. The untrained rows are random-projection sanity checks and cannot speak to convergence. The scale evidence covers three LLMs from two families, with size confounded by embedding dimension and head output size. There are no uncertainty estimates, a single seed (42), and rarity results rest on 20 proteins shown only in a figure.

versions.untested_parts: Tests LLM size within protein text/structure model pairs, with the GDM held fixed in Table 1; it does not test scale across independently trained models with varied objectives, data, and modalities generally, or directly measure general capability.
The study pairs protein text with protein structural representations; it does not test vision and language models on paired images and captions.
No comparison across random initialization seeds or shared subspaces across seeds is reported.

Tests learned linear projection heads for protein text and structure representations. It does not test stitching, relative representations, unpaired mapping, or interchangeability by downstream preservation under a direct loss measure.
No recurring interpretable features or circuits are identified or compared.

Tests alignment differences for popular versus rare proteins using the study's alignment score. It does not compare similarity metrics or settings such as neighbour count, and does not report out-of-distribution evaluation.

Shows incomplete and model-dependent alignment and discusses protein-data imbalance and homology. It does not establish a scale-related plateau or isolate shared training data/objectives as the cause across models.

relationships.reason: Held-out alignment rises monotonically with LLM size for each GDM (r01-r03, r07-r09, r10-r12). Gains are modest, and size is confounded with model family and embedding dimension.
relationships.display_finding: Held-out alignment rose monotonically but modestly with LLM size for each geometric model, with size confounded by family and embedding dimension.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: GearNet, ScanNet, GVP pairs with trained linear heads, LLM scaled from 2B to 70B
source_check.reason: Table 1 confirms monotonic increases for all three GDMs. Support is restricted to alignment after learned projections; size, embedding dimension and partly model family change together.

relationships.reason: Scores stay near zero (-0.053, -0.070, -0.061) at every LLM size, with no scale trend (r04-r06).
relationships.display_finding: Alignment scores stayed near zero at −0.053, −0.070 and −0.061, without an increasing size trend.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: r04-r06 show no increasing scale trend, and RQ1 explicitly describes ineffective alignment. An absent effect in this tested condition takes challenges under the verdict rules.

relationships.condition: GearNet, ScanNet, GVP pairs with a single linear head
relationships.reason: A linear map yields only modest held-out alignment (max 0.39, GVP ≤0.14) against an ideal near 1. The text also reports 2-layer heads clearly beat linear ones (Fig 4A, not in rows) (r01-r03, r07-r12).
relationships.display_finding: Held-out alignment scores reached at most 0.39 and no more than 0.14 for GVP against an ideal near 1, while two-layer heads clearly outperformed linear heads.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: GearNet, ScanNet, GVP pairs with a single linear head
source_check.reason: r01-r03 and r07-r12 measure positive-versus-negative cosine separation after two independently trained projection heads, one per modality. Distance from the ideal score does not quantify loss when replacing or reconstructing another model's representations; V4's low-loss interchangeability is untested.

relationships.reason: A trained linear map gives no alignment: negative-pair similarity exceeds positive, and scores stay near zero (r04-r06).
relationships.display_finding: Alignment scores stayed near zero, and negative-pair similarity exceeded positive-pair similarity.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.reason: r04-r06 establish failure of this contrastive alignment procedure. They do not test representation reconstruction or controlled interchangeability with little loss, so they cannot establish V4's absence.

relationships.condition: Popular vs rare proteins, non-GAT pairs
relationships.reason: The text reports popular proteins align better than rare ones, so measured alignment depends on the inputs. This rests on a figure with 10 proteins per group (r25-r26, r29-r34, r37-r42, r45-r48).
relationships.display_finding: In non-GAT comparisons, popular proteins aligned better than rare proteins, with 10 proteins per group.
